utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Registrar. I'd greet Mr. Scott, the Defence counsel, the accused, as well as everyone in this courtroom, and I'd like to greet our witness as well. As you know, sir, the examination-in-chief will now proceed. The Trial Chamber has decided to grant an additional 30 minutes to Mr. Scott, and of course the Defence will be granted 30 additional minutes as well for the purposes of the cross-examination. Since we have time on our hands because the cross-examination will continue tomorrow, we'll see as we proceed if we need to increase the time. Mr. Scott, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours, and to everyone in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And also to you, General. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: General, you've just heard that I'm in the final phase of my questions to you on behalf of the Prosecution and we're still continuing on the subject from yesterday afternoon or evening of issues or concerns about the presence of elements of the Croatian army in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and we were looking at some UN documents toward the end of the day. I would like to now show you, if you have -- I think you have the binder there. If you could please go to Exhibit 752.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, sir, my question to you and for the record this is a copy of Security Council Resolution 787, dated the 16th of November, 1992. Yesterday we briefly discussed some similar UN documents from earlier in 1992. Now we've arrived in November, and if I can just ask you to look briefly at paragraph numbered 5 on the third page of the document. And actually, if I can -- if I can -- let me modify my question to you. If I can first ask -- look to paragraph number 2 on the previous page. My apology, but if I can ask you first of all to go back to the previous page, number 2. It says "reaffirms that any taking of territory by force or any practice of ethnic cleansing is unlawful and unacceptable and will not be permitted to affect the outcome of the negotiations on constitutional arrangements ..." et cetera. General Pellnas, during the time of your association with the UN in this regard in the capacities as you've discussed yesterday, did you always understand it to be the position of the -- of the United Nations and indeed the international community, if you know, that the existing international -- internationally-recognised borders of Bosnia-Herzegovina were to be respected?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did you and other UNMOs and UNPROFOR always consider to be at least a part of your overall mandate to -- to monitor as part of your monitoring to ensure and to observe that those borders were in fact being respected?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at least it was not an obligation to report any breach what we could happen to detect.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, in terms of going back to paragraph number 5 on the next -- on the next page, and in particular it makes reference to its earlier Resolution 752, and at the end of that paragraph calls on in particular, including the "... requirement that all forces, in particular elements of the Croatian army, be withdrawn or be subject to the authority of the government of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina or be disbanded or disarmed." Can you confirm, General, by this and other documents that this continued to be an issue or concern throughout all of 1992 and into 1993?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could I ask you then to go to Exhibit 7789.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. So as not to waste any time, I'm going to put my question now. General, you have paragraph 5 in front of you. If we think of the previous resolution, the resolution we had a look at yesterday, number 752, dated 15th of May, whereas this particular resolution is resolution number 787, dated 16th of May, 1992. It was passed several months later. I notice that between paragraph 3 of Resolution 752 and paragraph 5 of Resolution 787, I note a slight variation that could be of interest. It is the fact that at paragraph 5 mention is made of the infiltration of units -- of irregular units and personnel, irregular units and personnel. This was not mentioned at paragraph 3 of Resolution 752. What does it mean according to you? Because in Resolution 752, the impression we got was that it was about the regular army of Croatia that was in theatre, whereas here we -- we mention irregular units. Do you have an idea about this particular point? Because as for me, I was quite struck when reading these two paragraphs in parallel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I'm not quite sure because it could easily be reference to Serb units working in the north-east part of -- of Bosnia. So I'm not sure to which the irregular units really refer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Thank you very much. Mr. Scott, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I could then ask you to go to 7789. And -- which is a statement by the president of the Security Council, dated the 3rd of February, 1994, and just briefly indicating and setting the context for some follow-up questions I will ask you about some more specific reports that were received following this -- this statement. Can you confirm, General Pellnas, that by this further statement by the Security Council in February 1994 that even by this time or by this time the same concern about the Croatian army's involvement in Bosnia-Herzegovina continued to be concern, in fact, may have become even a heightened concern by that time?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: How was the -- how was that particular issue, if you will, impacting or influencing the international community's dealings or relationships with Croatia during this time in general, late 1993, early 1994?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I want to comment on that because it's too complicated actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, also if I may go back to the previous answer that the gentleman said. He said "obviously." Was this looking at the document or "obviously" from his own knowledge? We can all read the document and draw our own conclusions but the question should be as to what he knows.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, given the issues that you were involved in during this time, I'm simply asking based on your experiences in dealing with various issues on the ground during this time is what is reflected in Exhibit 7789, concern -- disconcern about the Croatian army. Was that consistent with the issues that you were dealing with in general?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, you said the issue was too complicated. I'm going to have to press you - General, my apologies - a bit because based again on your experience you can tell us presumably, hopefully if I can say following on your words a simplified version that this particular matter that is the concern about the presence of Croatian troops in Bosnia was affecting the international politics and dealings at this time. Was there -- had sanctions been threatened against Croatia at any time; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I would object to leading. He's asked the question and now he's giving answers to the witness. Let the witness answer the question or rephrase the question. Let's do it step-by-step, but let's not ask a question then feed an answer and then ask for a verification of the answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My hesitance is -- pardon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, as far as possible, please try not to lead the witness. Do as I do myself. Put a general question first.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I did, Your Honour, and I was trying to follow up on the witness's obvious reluctance when he said it's a very complicated issue and I was trying to encourage him forward but I think the witness is prepared to answer the best as he can.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm very hesitant to answer it because it will lead me into discussions about the great powers politics on the Balkans.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. That's exactly what we need to hear because this is what we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Is this comment called for now Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: No, I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But I haven't finished. I haven't finished though. It became obvious much later on that there was -- I mean, the united States versus Croatia is complicated during this time. On the one hand they really want the Federation to take shape and there be success and have the united Bosnia. On the other hand, they are training Croatian officers for the war against the Serbs in Krajina. So what the international community really thought and did about Croatia is a very complicated thing. It depends on what part of international community we discuss and then what context we discuss it. So that explains my hesitance to give a simple answer to this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Based on that, Your Honour, I ask that we explore this area completely because of the nature and the breadth of the indictment because Croatia is being attacked, is being involved in a joint criminal enterprise by way of its leader, then President Tudjman. I think now for the first time we have someone who is going to unfold the story a little bit. We're going to unpeel the onion as it were. So I suggest we go into this full throttle.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, again, Your Honour, if Mr. Karnavas wants to use his cross-examination to do that, he can seek to do that. I think it would be -- many parts of what he's just said would be completely irrelevant. But if he wants to spend his cross-examination doing that then he may do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: General, no one ever suggested, at least, lest of all me, that this was necessarily a simple issue. I just asked if you could confirm that part of the mix, if you will, of this complicated factor the involvement of Croatia in Bosnia-Herzegovina was part of the -- what was on the international table at the time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you please to go to Exhibit P -- well, excuse me, 7889?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And just to follow up in terms of -- this is a letter from the Secretary-General at the time of Boutros Boutros-Ghali reporting again various information that had been gathered by UNPROFOR troops -- excuse me, the presence of the Croatian army in Bosnia during this time, and, for instance, mentioned several times --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do apologise, but as far as I can see this is document 7889 and as far as I can see that document is not on our chart, and I notice that the other Defence teams don't seem to have it, and yesterday the Prosecutor also showed a document that we didn't have on our chart, but we didn't react to that, but I must say that we can't follow unless we have received the documents. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, let me just check our records, Your Honour. I'm not sure why that might be the case, but if it is -- if there's been an error, there's been an error.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: While we're looking at that document, then, sir, and it was primarily to provide in fact the further context of the next document. Can I ask you to look then at Exhibit 7915. If you can go to 7915 and if we can solve the matter of the previous document we'll come back to it. Sir, this document and the next couple of exhibits I'm going to show you if you will are all part of a single package that essentially revolve around or link to Exhibit 7915. This is a report dated the 20th of February, 1994, from UN military observers on the withdrawal of HV forces from Bosnia. In the first paragraph of the document under "Discussion" it says, "UNMO BH south did so and observed some equipment withdrawing from the Buna area." Now this is the same UNMO BH south that we've been talking about previously in your testimony as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. This is -- I had left, and I don't know who were actually serving at the BH south.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you know --

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: But it is the same organisation of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, that was my question to you. Do you know of any other UNMO organisation that was operating in that region at that time?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And in the next paragraph it says, "On the 18th of February, UNMOs were denied access to sections of the HVO area of responsibility between Buna and Stolac." Again, is that again continuing on from where we left off yesterday in terms of throughout 1993 one of the recurring issues with the UN military observers and UNPROFOR was freedom of movement and access to the territory?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the gentleman just indicated that he had left. So I don't see how he can comment on this document or on the events over there. I just point this out. So maybe with some foundation he might be able to comment, but based on this document he just indicated. So I don't mean to be obstreperous or maybe you know it seems that way but I don't mean to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think the document stands by itself, actually. It's a very clear report. And freedom of movement was denied by all parties in all places all during the mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well. And when it says, for example, in the end of the -- excuse me just a moment. I lost my place, to be honest. In the first paragraph just in terms of UNMO and UNPROFOR procedure, it says this -- the letter is attached. I'm going to come back to that in a moment, but this letter was faxed to UNMO headquarters BH command and to UNMO sector BH south. UNMO headquarters BH command confirmed that headquarter BH command issued a tasking to SpaBat to pick at the main Buna-Metkovic road arteries, I think, and I agree that the document's -- during this -- during the scheduled withdrawal period, UNMO BH south. Is that -- is that the procedure that will be followed in terms of the chain of command from UNMO -- through the UNMO command structure?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't find the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In the first paragraph, sir. 7915.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: First paragraph. Halfway through the first paragraph it talks about putting --

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Just -- let me read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if they really want to know what the procedure is they can ask the gentleman what the procedure is. If this a way of getting the document in, again, I stand by my earlier objection to which I did not receive a ruling from the Bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Karnavas, you're absolutely right. Mr. Scott, the witness was not aware of this document because he told us that at the time he'd already left. He'd already left this post.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] However -- however, there might be a number of control and observation procedures outlined in this document. What do you want to set out in this document? Is it the tenor of this document? But that could be commented upon by other people. Or do you want to point out what the procedures were?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Both, Your Honour, and let me say that this man is in a perfectly good condition to explain. He knows the issue generally. He's talked about it yesterday and today, that he's familiar with the issue of the concern, the continuing concern from 1992 to 1994 about the presence of the Croatian army in Bosnia. He has talked about his responsibilities. By this time he was continuing as the military advisor to Stoltenberg. He was the principal military advisor to the conference on the former Yugoslavia, and still involved in these issues and very knowledgeable of UNMO and UNPROFOR procedure. I think that puts him in a completely suitable position to explain to us aspects of the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've been observing the witness. He's studying the document as if he's about to give oral examinations. And there's nothing wrong with that but it would appear to me that the gentleman has never seen the document. Therefore, I don't know how he's able to comment about the contents of the document itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'm going to put the question myself. We don't want to be wasting any time. General, Mr. Scott has just said that you were the military advisors of -- to Lord Owen. That fact given to us by Mr. Scott. And as military advisors, you certainly had a general knowledge of the military matters in Bosnia. Therefore, I'd like to put to you the following important question: Were the negotiators aware of the presence of elements of the Croatian army in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was it an observation that had been transmitted or conveyed to the observers? You say yes, but can you please expand on your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my work at the international conference we also received the daily reports from -- situation reports from UNPROFOR, as well as the UNMO situation report, and we followed up on them every morning. So whatever was reported by UNMOs and UNPROFOR, we knew of it even if we did not perhaps follow it in such a detail as one did in UNPROFOR because we had a lot of other things to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if you can then just assist us in various parts of this report then and based on your knowledge. The first -- going back to the first paragraph with this background in mind, it says: "On the 15th of February, 1994, UNMO Dubrovnik received a letter from southern sector CA authorities." Now, could I ask you to look at 10011, which in fact appears to be a letter to -- in the upper-left corner you will see "UNMO Dubrovnik." Indeed the 15th of February, 1994, from a Croatian army general, apparently Marinovic. I need to point out a couple of documents to you before I can then put my final couple of questions to you about this. Keeping that document in mind, if you go back to Exhibit 7915, to the second paragraph, please, the one that begins the 18th of February -- "On 18 February." In that paragraph you'll see a reference to "See UNMO report attached (IN.327)." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you confirm to the Judges that UNMO reports were numbered in such a fashion?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't remember how they were numbered.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You don't remember. All right. Can I ask you to look at Exhibit 10013.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can ask you to look, please, to the up -- far upper-left corner of Exhibit 10013. Do you see the number --

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you to go to the next paragraph of 7915, the report, which says: "On the 18th of February, another letter was received from southern sector CA headquarters." And can I ask you, please, to look at Exhibit 10012. And do you see that that is in fact a letter to UNMO Dubrovnik, indeed dated 18 February 1994, from a Croatian army officer, apparently Mihocevic.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And finally, if you look at the next paragraph of the report, it says: "On 19 February, UNMOs conducted more patrols into the HVO AOR. See UNMO report attached (IN.356)." And if I can ask you to look, please, at Exhibit 7913. If you have that, sir, can I again ask you to look in the upper left corner of that document and is that UNMO report -- does that UNMO report in fact bear the number IN.356?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In the second of the two letters from the Croatian army officer, the one that is Exhibit 10012, the officer Mihocevic appears to be complaining that to their -- to the Croatian army's disappointment, no one was there to see them when they withdrew. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell again based on what we've covered this morning and the reason for asking you these questions what was the situation generally as you recall at the time if you can give us some assistance. Why would the Croatian -- why would the Croatian army wanted to have been seen withdrawing from Bosnia and Herzegovina by the international community at this time?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose that this was a time when the federation was born. So I suppose Zagreb had every reason to appear to cooperate. That's my only explanation why they were eager to -- to make sure that it was well-known that they withdraw.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: General Pellnas, that concludes my questions. I want to thank you very much for coming to The Hague and giving your testimony.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, for the additional time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation] Who is going to start Mr. Ibrisimovic? I'm turning to the Defence. Who would like to start?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... for this witness and we give our time to the other Defence teams. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. For Mr. Coric. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. Could I please ask the usher to come and collect our binders, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General. Whilst we're waiting for the binders to be distributed, I will have a couple of questions by way of an introduction. And I will be dealing solely with joint police patrols you mentioned yesterday, and I believe we will be finished quite soon. Yesterday, you told us in your testimony at pages 39, 41, and 42 of the record, of the transcript, that joint police patrols operated on a 24-hour basis, and that discussions on the patrols started on the 20th of April in Mostar, and that on the 21st of April, 1993, you visited the location where the joint patrol was stationed at. You told us that you came across soldiers there and not policemen. You also told us that this was one of the things that disappointed you. The first question I should like to put to you is the following: When you say -- or when you refer to joint police patrols, did you mean joint police patrols of the military police or joint police patrols of the civilian police? What -- what was it that you expected to find there?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I expected to find normal police, civilian police. The word "military police" was never mentioned or discussed.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I should like to move on to the documents now. Before you you have a binder of documents. Their Honours also have hard copies, and we have also distributed them to the interpreters' booths so that we don't have to wait for them to show up on e-court. Let us first look at document 5D 02052.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Say again, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: 5D 02052. That's the last document in your binder. This document is dated the 21st of April, 1993. This is the report on the work of the mixed group of the BH army and HVO. I will read out only the first sentence on page 1 and the last line at page 1 in the English version, as well as page 2. And these passages are the same in the Croatian version as well. The first sentence of the document reads as follows: "On the 21st of April, 1993, the mixed patrol of the ABiH and HVO that had the task to maintain public law and order in the city of Mostar, and which was located in the building of Vodoprivreda of the HZ HB hereby submits the following report." I will move on to that other sentence, which is in the last line on that page. "At 0710 hours on the 21st of April, 1993, General Pellnas arrived again, and he was informed of all the events that had taken place during the night. He finds the action successful, and thinks, believes, that his -- that this kind of work should continue until -- until a more stable solution is found. The main conclusion of the joint patrol is that tasks and powers for the tasks should be given immediately in a written form so that it could work efficiently." Signed on behalf of the HVO by Zarko Juric and on behalf of the ABiH Esad Humo and Goran Jelavic. Tell me, sir, is this document referring to that visit of yours that you described for us when you went to that location and met with members of the joint patrol?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the first time I see the document, but obviously it refers to my visit to the -- what I called the joint police.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us please look at another document, which is 2D 00313, and that's the penultimate document in your binder.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: This is a joint public announcement which was drafted by the commander of the forced corps -- the 4th Corps of the ABiH army, Arif Pasalic, and the chief of operation zone south-east Herzegovina, Petar Zelenika. The public announcements states at the very beginning: "Today on the 21st of April, 1993," and so on and so forth. And let us look at Item 4, please, which reads: "Joint teams of the military police will be formed and will perform their duties once the conclusion contained in item 1 is implemented," and I will not read it now but it refers -- it refers to the withdrawal of the armies into their respective barracks. Please tell me, did you see this release, press release, at the time you were in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: But you are familiar with Mr. Pasalic and Mr. Zelenika. You know who they were?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Please let us look at document P 02030 now. This is the first document in your binder. This is an order by the commander of the operations zone of East Herzegovina, brigadier Miljenko Lasic, dated the 22nd of April, 1993. The operation zone of South-east Herzegovina. Let us look at item 8 which is on page 2 in the English version, which reads: "Joint HVO military police and BH army teams shall be established to carry out around-the-clock patrols of all parts of the city and to control the situation." Tell me, did you see this document while you were in Mostar? And were you aware of this order?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware of part of it, but I think I only got it in verbal version. For example, "That all members should be forbidden to wear black uniform," which was a reaction of myself coming and complaining about the special unit at Hotel Ero. And I found it a bit ridiculous, and at the time when they said that all units should not -- be forbidden to wear black uniforms, because I never believed it was an HVO unit anyway. I have seen another document, I believe, but not this one. There -- there was a document, and it may well be here.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: No, it is not here. Let me tell you why I'm asking you all of this. Let me tell you one thing, and I'm saying this for the sake of the Trial Chamber and everyone else in the courtroom, that on the 13th of February, 2007, Witness A was examined here. He was a member of the military police of the ABiH, and he told us that once the agreement was reached joint military police patrols were formed. He was a member of one such patrol as a member of the military police of the BH army. He told us that the patrols were operational until the 7th or the 8th of May, 1993. He said that the part of the patrol that consisted of members of the BH army was housed in the SDK building. He indicated that they went about performing their duties in -- as per normal, that they had to take off all of their military insignia, and that they were distinguished from others -- from other soldiers merely by wearing white belts. The question I have for you now is the following: When you visited the building where these joint patrols were located, you actually saw members of the military police there and not just ordinary soldiers, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time I could see no difference or did not observe any difference, which is -- I saw them as military personnel, or what I saw them as, but my first and most important impression was that they were not there to do any job at all. And during the days I spent in Mostar, no patrolling took place. If that was the case afterwards, I cannot comment upon.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: You told us that the patrols were operational for 24 hours only. I paraphrased a statement by a witness, a member of the BH army, who was a member of these patrols and who stated before the Trial Chamber that they performed their duties until the 7th or 8th of May, 1993. Let us look at the last document you have in the binder there, which is document number P 02192. And can we move into closed session whilst we're dealing with this document, because this is a SpaBat document, which is under seal, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document is under seal. We therefore need to move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who is next? Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I will be next, Mr. President. I'll need a couple of minutes to -- well, a minute to set up, and the usher can get the documents. May I begin? Once again good morning, Mr. President, good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good morning, General. My name is Michael Karnavas. With me is Ms. Suzana Tomanovic, and we represent Jadranko Prlic. I have four or five areas that I want to cover, but first I thought we would go through some housekeeping matters. In looking at your statements, you gave four statements, two of which are related more or less to this case. Would that be correct? One being on the -- the 19th to 22nd of June, 1999, and the second one being -- I believe it was in 4 to 5 December 2001.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you say so, yes. I don't remember the dates, and I don't have the papers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Were you given an opportunity to review your statements, by the way, and when you arrived here at The Hague?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have reviewed them, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And you also published a book, I guess in -- in Swedish.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: "Utan Slut", is that --

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Without End," yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And I just want to cover a couple of points real quickly first of all, because my client's name, Dr. Jadranko Prlic, comes up. May I ask first and foremost how much time, actual time did you spend with him discussing any matters?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very will time. We had lunch together on one occasion as I remember, but I don't remember when. It was probably before the events in Mostar, which are described in my book.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then I met him on a meeting at the hospital, and then I just had this very short encounter in hotel Ana Marija when he said hello.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Is it fair to say in April 1993 when you went into Mostar you did not have any in-depth conversations with him?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And aside from seeing him on that one particular day when you arrived at -- I guess it was the hospital, the Mostar hospital, you did not have any further contact with him the following days that you were in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And if we could fast forward, when you did run into him, and I believe those were your terms on one of your statements, you said you ran into him in Medjugorje, that would have been, I believe, in February 1990 --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: He wasn't -- he didn't attend a meeting there?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was in company with some individuals at the hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. He wasn't accompanied, but my question was that he did not attend the meeting. He was not there as part of any meeting?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know in what capacity he was there but certainly not a meeting with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Exactly. And you didn't have any discussions with him other than him coming up to you?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And it was him that made the initiation to come up to you and to greet with you -- to greet you?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember how we met, if he was going out or if he just came up. I can't tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And -- and now you say, because I don't see this anywhere else in your -- in your statements or your book, that you believe you might have had lunch with him prior to, I suspect, April 1993.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. I might have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Have I a vague recollection, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- I won't comment on it. We had lunch on one occasion, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But I take it the lunch was rather -- well, for lack of a better term, was not terribly memorable?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, it was. I remember him well from the time -- from the lunch.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But I mean -- okay. All right.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a social event.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It was a social event, okay. The reason I mention this is because you describe him as the self-proclaimed Prime Minister, and this would have been back in April 1993. Did you actually know what his title was? You say he was a self-Prime Minister of Herceg-Bosna. I mean, if you don't know that's fine.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must admit I haven't seen any formal documents describing his title. He was referred to as the Prime Minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now when you say he was referred to, referred to by whom?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: By almost everybody --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- around.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And I take it when you say "everybody", those who were speaking a language which you understood.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of them, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And -- and it was on that one occasion, the first occasion in April you describe where the meeting was interrupted. Yesterday, you said after Mr. Stojic left that -- I believe you used the word Mr. Prlic excused --

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- although I believe somewhere in your book you say that he stood up and apologised.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, apologised. I meant that when I say excused.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, during that meeting he was polite?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And he wasn't sarcastic or scornful in any way?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you say you ran into him in Medjugorje and here's where I have -- you know, I must say I have some -- some reservations about some of your characterisations. You say that he was -- were some folks that were wearing black jackets, but then at one point you describe him as sort of -- I believe it was in your second statement, the perfect style Mafia man, and then later on --

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- you're referring to the men in black.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I see. Okay. Would it be fair to say that a lot of people in the former Yugoslavia wear black jackets?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. That is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: But just let me then clarify that it was my very definite impression that the person he was sitting with were criminals and from that I was back to my other experience and I still believe they were criminals.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. You didn't know them?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You didn't speak to them?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You didn't have them investigated?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But this was an impression that you formed?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I got the strong impression that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You got a strong impression?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That was based on what they were wearing?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was based on how they looked and how they were dressed and how they behaved and what I know from previous occasions and other people and other corners on the Balkans so that created the impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The impression.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: And it is just an impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. And one might say that as far as you were concerned they were also in bad taste, stylistic taste?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. One other matter I just wanted to bring up before we go into other areas. You indicated in your book that you met Mate Boban on two occasions, at least, the first time was in Zagreb and that would have been I believe on the 17th of April, correct, 1993?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And it was a short meeting. I believe it was at the Intercontinental?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And at that point I believe you described him as sort of being like the perfect hotel manager type, cordial, convivial?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, he looked very amicable, yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And then I noticed that when you describe him again the second time that you meet him, and this would have been a few days later, which is when you say that at that point in time at that second meeting, I believe it was the 22nd or the 23rd of April, that you finally understood what he was trying to convey to you back in Zagreb, at that point you sort of described him as being or looking like a godfather with bodyguards that were -- and you described them as gorillas. That kind of struck me because again it seems that you're rather harsh with your characterisations, your impressions, your first impressions. Could you expand on that a little bit?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, when you write books you have a freedom to phrase yourself a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Secondly, it was hard not to find this phrase, because if you see a man coming up with two 700 BMWs wearing a silk suit and having four enormously impressive bodyguards jumping out in front you it was very close to see what I described.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a definition of what I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Is it fair to say however, because I worked in Bosnia and I used to work under an ambassador, that they normally go around with what they called CPUs, close protection unit and some of those folks look pretty big, no?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That he true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The whole purpose is if you are going to be a bodyguard, you have to look rather impressive, no? Sort of like me, would not make a big impression on anybody.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. But if you take a timid man in Intercont and the man coming out in a silk suit out of 2 BMWs 700 with four very big bodyguards it gets another impression and that's what I have written about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. May I ask you, was that impression formed at that moment or was it formed, you know, did it cogitate in your mind and as you were sitting there in France writing the book you know, searching for ways to describe the -- the scene?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think it -- the impression was born at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And the reason I'm asking is because if you see somebody who purportedly is there on behalf of, you know, as the -- as the president and you have this impression, might that have coloured your opinion of anything that he might have been trying to convey?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would put it the other way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I stood by my first impression writing the book because of what I later learnt --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- about the area and the role of Mr. Boban.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it verified and sort of gave me the right to write this piece.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, on both occasions, we're going to get a little ahead of ourselves, but on both occasions, I want to cover what Mr. Boban was trying to convey to you. As I understand, it was -- what he was trying to say that the way he envisaged the situation between the Croats and the Muslim armies, that is, that they could co-exist and fight against the common enemy, which would have been the Serbs, would have been north of a particular area. The -- the Croats would be subordinated to the Muslim army and south of that line and vice versa. Would that being correct?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a possible interpretation of what Mr. Boban said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I did not believe in them and the events following when they actually did not fight the Serbs but the Muslim gave me some vindification for my idea to see what he actually proposed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, we're going to take it one step at a time because you say that your impression -- at least in your book you say that your impression was that he was proposing a division of Bosnia but then later on you say he asked you to work out an appropriate solution to make a proposal to Lord Owen.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So the context in which he was telling you these things was for you as a military man, him being a politician, and let's face it, sometimes politician may have ideas but military folks have to implement those ideas in the field and the military men are the most capable of determining what is and is not feasible, he was then asking you to then go to Lord Owen, another politician, if it -- or --

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- political individual --

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yep, yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- or civilian to make a proposal to Lord Owen, who at the time, and correct me if I'm wrong, at the time was engaged in the Vance-Owen peace process; correct?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I didn't take it seriously because I had no connection whatsoever with David Owen at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, when you say -- now, I agree with you on that one. Did you communicate that to Mr. Boban and say, you know, thank you very much, but I don't -- I don't have a brief with Mr. Owen?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think Mr. Boban knew exactly what low rank I had for the moment in my position and that I had no connection with the Vance-Owen group.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. You say --

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: So I found it completely unnecessary to define my role.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, you say low rank. First of all, you were a general. Second of all, you were a foreigner. Third, you were with the UN. And fourth, you were in Zagreb. And you did have a rather high position within the UN. Would you not say that?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So you weren't such a low individual?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, comparatively, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Comparatively. Well, if I may say so, I've been observing you. You don't -- you don't carry yourself like you're low profile?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's because I'm old.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I don't think so. I think from reading what you went -- when you went down to Mostar, you're a man of action?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So perhaps he may have come to you because he thought that you might have been able to assist. Did that -- did that ever cross your mind?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now, you indicated to us that you were not involved in the Vance-Owen Peace Plan. May I ask, may I ask were you at the time keeping up with what was happening with those negotiations in any detail?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not really, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not really. I had the general viewpoint but not in detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I take it Vance-Owen, or Mr. Vance and Mr. Owen, did not in any way brief -- brief your department as far as what they were doing or what they were trying to achieve?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that part of the Vance-Owen peace process, it wasn't just trying to find a political solution for Bosnia and Herzegovina but also how the militaries could work together? There was all sorts of different components to that.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I say obviously because I was pulled in in Zagreb on a meeting when they were there to present some sort of military.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Exactly. Now I think you said it was in one of your statements you said it was April 30th?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: 30th, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But could it have been April 24th? Could you be mistaken on that particular day?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could be mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And that was the first time as I understand it, and correct me if I'm wrong, that was the first time when you were pulled in that you were either engaged in, a participant of, or an observer of the process one of the three?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Did they actually, at that particular time, ask you to -- to engage yourself at that moment or at some other -- or was it at some other point?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was -- I don't know if it was the day before or in the morning it was Brigadier John Wilson who called me and asked me to come and --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- tried to help to present some sort of formula for the military cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, them asking you that, that was based on your limited knowledge of what was happening in the field. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you wanted to mention -- name it, limit it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I don't want to put words in your mouth, but you term -- in your book you talk about what lessons you could draw from your excursion. That was the word that you used and I actually went up and I looked at the word excursion on the dictionary to make sure, and you seem to be a man who chooses his words rather well, but that in essence was your entire, up until that point, involvement in working between the Croats and the Muslims in trying to find a solution among themselves; correct?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I came down in late October to the area, and I took up office on -- in November, early November. So I had been in the States for a couple of months before this happened, almost half a year.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. But you were in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not very much time in Zagreb. I was most of the time in Bosnia, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And were you in -- in the Mostar area dealing with Croat-Muslim issues?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not before then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay not before then. So when I'm saying -- when you refer to your excursion, the -- the universe, if you want to put it that way, of your experience, hands on experience, in dealing with Croat-Muslim problems, was that period when you went in April 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And as I understand from reading your statements, when Mr. Ganic showed up you did not expect him.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And he introduce -- he was introduced to you, I believe, by General --

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Wahlgren.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- Wahlgren?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: As a vice-president of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yep, yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Would it surprise you, sir, if I were to tell you that at that point in time such a position did not exist in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wouldn't surprise me a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. He was a member of the Presidency. You had heard of the Presidency; correct?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And you're shaking your head. We need to make a record.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And as I understand it, later on when you went to Mostar, you also met a gentleman, although we don't see it anywhere in your report perhaps because he didn't make much of an impression, Mr. Franjo Boras. Do you recall him?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember him from the meeting. It is a possibility that I actually had lunch with him, but I don't remember the name. If -- if you will present me with a photograph of him, I will -- I can possibly identify him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I think he's a short wiry type of fellow who is probably older than you at the time.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In that case he still is if he's still alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And -- and he was a member of the Presidency, by the way.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And he also had equal rank, if you will, with -- with Mr. Ganic. Okay. Were you aware of that at the time?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Did Mr. Ganic introduce to you and say here is my colleague from the Presidency --

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Were you aware that he had come up from Sarajevo? Mr. Boras, that is.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, as I understand it, before we get to your impressions of Mr. Ganic, at some point, be it as it may, based on the conversations that were being held at the time, you were asked to go -- to go down into the Mostar area because meetings were taking place; correct?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And as I understand it, you did not have any particular mission, as it were. And I use the word "mission" because I think military folks like to work with missions. You know, they want to know what the term -- the terms of engagement are and what have you. So you didn't have a brief in a sense; right?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was not a very well-formulated task.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. But you being a general, being in the military, being a sort of action man, you went down there and sort of seized the situation, as it were, and tried to take some action, what you believed to be appropriate under the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course I went with the general understanding that there was maybe a conflict coming, and our task was to do whatever we could to avoid that conflict, to go into reality, so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Had you been told by the way from Mr. Ganic and others that there had already been an ongoing process in theatre, if you want to call it that, whereby the European Monitors, the ECMM, were at the time engaged with both parties in trying to figure out ways that would implement the Vance-Owen peace process?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was extremely poorly briefed about the ECMM undertakings in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you think, and I'm asking you now to speculate. I might be drawing an objection, but do you think Mr. Ganic would have known what was happening in the field before he set out to meet with you to ask you, the UN that is, to come down and sort things out?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he anyway said that he had had consultations with Mr. Boban.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: And they were in agreeance on the necessity to create good conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. And I don't want to go into the meetings too much because others may cover it, but if we could go through some -- some of the documents, but before we do that, you described -- you spent some time with Mr. Ganic on a one-on-one; correct?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Much more time than you did, for instance, with Mr. Prlic?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. You were able to sort of glean the type of person he was?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had described at least his outer behaviours and looks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. He spoke English?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Had been trained in America or educated in America or worked in America?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But he spoke enough English for you to communicate in that same language?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And you said that he wasn't very talkative but rarely explicit. That's one way you've put it.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And then you said that --

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: He made very -- if I use the word nervous, it's a bit like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unsteady.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Unsteady.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You also say he was volatile, incoherent, unrealistic. You gave us a description of what Misa Glenny -- how he characterised him as suffering from --

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that was deeply unjustified.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But you also said he was characterised as a fanatical Muslim and an extremist?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some people claim that he was. I found no verification of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Just about the record. Suffering from something you were saying, but it is not in the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Incipient senility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Senility. It was just awkward to have nothing in the transcript and then a comment on that by General --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. And of course you -- you're not a psychologist or psychiatrist, you didn't psycho-analyse that these were some of the impressions?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you ever, by the way, read Lord Owen's book on Mr. Ganic?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Were you aware and perhaps we could just go through this very quickly. I don't want to spend too much time on it but I think it might be important on a global text -- for global reasons. 1D 01547. This is an excerpt. I have three short excerpts from David Owen's book, and on page 89 of that book, and I'll read from the middle of the page, he said -- well, he characterises him first as being the most complex person in the Bosnian government. But later on he says: "He was one -- he has one central policy objective, namely to involve the US army as a combatant in the Bosnian fight to defeat the Serbs, as he sees it, to achieve this aim of which he makes no secret. He's entitled to use whatever means are necessary. To him the ends justify those means. He orchestrates Bosnian government propaganda operating at every level in the US, at the white house or capitol hill and on the television screens in American homes." Then later on - I'll skip one sentence - he goes on to say: "There is a doggedness about his character that shows itself in his readiness to spend much time in Sarajevo and take the risks of its citizens, but the focus of his attention and his travel is on the US. He knows that you have to spend money to be heard in America and is ready, therefore, to employ media consultants and use all the modern techniques of communications." And then it goes on. I don't want to spend too much more time, but did you -- were you aware of these qualities of Mr. Ganic?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, anyway, I saw him very often on American television.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I take it he was promoting his --

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- point of view.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now if we could turn to another section of Mr. -- Mr. Owen's book. And this I'm referring to now is 1D 01548.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yeah, 1548.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yep. I now realise I have read -- I have read the "Balkan Odyssey".

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. It's hard to --

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a thick book.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You got to know Mr. Owen, did you not?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, rather well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rather well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Would you say he was a serious individual?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are talking about the former Foreign Minister of United Kingdom, Great Britain. So he is serious.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. We have two fellas from the UK so they are happy to hear these words. I hear the chuckling. If we could just probably to save time just go to -- flip the page and go to 220 in the middle of the passage, because this is a lengthy letter that was sent by Mr. Owen, and in the middle of it he says: "My biggest fear is not how the Serbs are reacting but that such talk will encourage Ganic and others who want to continue with the war that the Americans are about to intervene. Ganic certainly is attempting to derail the negotiations and is hoping for airstrikes. He may even now be seeing -- we may even be seeing a slowing in the tempo of the negotiations because of the NAC meetings -- meeting. Izetbegovic is talking openly about needing four to five days more for negotiations. Silajdzic and others here have been most unhelpful and have not been trying to -- and have been trying to undermine Izetbegovic's negotiating position, but so far to no avail." Now -- and this is the autumn of 1993 in the book. Were you aware that Mr. Ganic was sort of engaged in this sort of a -- these sorts of tactics? I know you talked about it yesterday. At some point the Muslims for sure did not want to end the war because they were gaining ground, but were you aware that this was happening?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there was a constant effort from the Izetbegovic side and people around him to bring in an active participation, at least to have arms, and working on the media and public opinion in the United States, and I think they were very skilful at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And did you notice by any chance when you were in the field, in theatre, that at some point there was a shift in -- from the Vance-Owen Peace Plan to sort of an American approach in trying to find a solution?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. I would say when the Contact Group really came in the international conference of the former Yugoslavia was more or less brushed aside during the summer of 1994. That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- that's why I had the opportunity to write the book, because we went out of work for a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But because you were out of work you're not now somehow tailoring your answers. In other words, your observations were based on what was happening as opposed to maybe harbouring some animosity towards the Americans for ending your mission?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have no animosity. I just state the fact that the Contact Group suddenly came in with a big effort and made a real impact and they brushed us aside.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We became politically unimportant during this period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we could look at just one last document on this issue and that's 1D 01549. Again, from Mr. Owen's book. And this would be on page 236. We see the date above it is 30th September. This is towards the third paragraph on the page, and I'm just going to read sort of in the middle of that paragraph. It says: "Our own reporting showed that Izetbegovic had appeared to be in the pro-peace camp but had never championed it. His performance was low-key and detached at all times. Ganic's position was very hardline. It had been strikingly noticeable that he continued to talk about the need for land on the sea and was not satisfied with a proposed solution of Ploce and a port on the Neretva." We can go on further down. He says -- we pick up where it he says: "Silajdzic was apparently trying to reach a deal with the Croats having spent two weeks in Zagreb talking with Foreign Minister Mate Granic to get a proposed Muslim-Croat working group off the ground, being aware that at one stage the SDA leaders had come very close to declaring a Muslim state." Were you aware that this was -- that this was an ongoing process while you were trying to find a solution, you and others, that you had Mr. Ganic, who appeared nervously to you, or was nervous when he came up, perhaps maybe that was part of his tatoi, you know, part of his shtick as we say, to appear nervous and timid?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nervous is not the correct translation of what I mean in Swedish.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you mean nervous, anxious I don't mean that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Were you aware that this was Mr. Ganic's --

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm becoming very inconvenient with what you're asking me now. You had the great objections that I should comment upon UN resolutions. Now you ask me to comment upon "Balkan Odyssey" by Lord Owen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm asking you to comment about an individual that you spend time with --

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- and you characterise him in various fashions and I'm asking you whether you were --

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think Lord Owen can speak for himself and the text is there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But were you aware that this was happening behind your back at least, that this was an agenda?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The whole world was happening behind my back of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was an enormous amount of polititians, military men and states involved in the Balkan drama. And if you believed that you knew what was going on -- nobody knew actually what was going on, not even the big players I guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And I mention all this because we're going to get into some other areas, but in your own book, you talk about being politically naive. This is from your lessons that you learned apparently from your excursion.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. And I meant that we -- I at least completely underestimated the width of the contradictions in the Mostar area. It was far deeper than I thought when I went down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Because you say we were far too ignorant or at leave I was of the political game that was being played.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It should have been much better prepared.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Would it be correct to say that one way of getting better prepared would have been, for instance, to have become more familiar with what was happening in the Vance-Owen peace process, so at least you would have known what the two parties were being asked to do and what the two parties were doing with the peace negotiators? Would that have been helpful? In hindsight, of course?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course, the more you know about what is going politically the better you will act as a military man also in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the other hand, one solution I gave to Wahlgren afterwards was that UNPROFOR should have established a territorial system with experienced officers. In that case you would have had a brigadier general in the Mostar area --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- working with the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm about to start a new chapter. Perhaps we could take a break at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'm told that I used up 36, was it? Thirty-eight, 38 minutes. I was told that I was getting 15 minutes from one of the teams. I think it was the Pusic team. So that would give me 45 by your calculation. I would be asking Your Honours to allow me to do -- to have a full hour, you know, starting from now. But if that's not the case, then I would like some guidance as to how much time the Trial Chamber's willing to give me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You want one hour starting from now? Well, please proceed then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We'll move rather quickly, General, and hopefully we won't use up the whole hour. I want to -- I have a couple of documents going -- referring to April 1993. If we could go to document 1D 01546, 1546.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If you could look at that. You will see that it says at the top that this is a weekly summary report, 28 of March to 3 April 1993. It appears to be generated from HQ ECMM. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And of course you're familiar with the fact that this -- the -- the headquarters of the ECMM would have been in Zenica -- or the regional centre was in Zenica; correct?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just two brief matters. If we just look at sort of the last paragraph, it says: "The Muslim authorities have, however, continued their negotiations with Bosnian Croats in order to reach a common agreement on a joint military command." And I merely point this out because it would appear at least as early as this particular week there were discussions ongoing between the Croats and the Muslims to try to reach some accommodation for joint command structure; correct?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no comment on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
