utterances.text: Okay. Very well. Well, was this brought to your attention by the ECMM?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I -- I only knew about the contacts through what Ganic said about his contacts with Mate Boban.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now Just very briefly, when you did arrive in Mostar on the 18th, I believe, you indicated that the hearing -- or the meeting had already started, and it was Mr. -- or Ambassador Thebault; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: He was the head of the ECMM?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Zenica regional centre, I guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, due to the circumstances because a lot of things were happening at the time, I realise that you were very busy, did you have an opportunity to actually discuss with Mr. Thebault what the ECMM might have been doing prior to your arrival in facilitating the process between the two parties?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. If we could flip to the next page very briefly, because it says here: "The Mostar authorities are also developing an overall negotiations offer concerning the future organisation of the republic. HCC Grude has so been approached at the level of Mr. Prlic, president of HVO, who overhands a proposal made some days before by Mr. Maric to propose to ECMM to play a mediation role in negotiations which could be led not only with the Muslim community but also with the Bosnian Serb government. HRC should meet Mr. Prlic and members of its government next Thursday after their weekly meeting in order to make its proposal more precise." Were you aware of this -- this process, sir?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I say before, only through what I learnt from Mr. Ganic. I also understood that there had been discussions between Tudjman and Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. Okay. But as far as Mr. -- I notice that in your book you make a -- you describe an ECMM monitor from the UK, someone who was handsome but also had a knack for aggravating or infuriating folks, be they Croat, Serb or Muslim.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was a nasty comment on my part.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But I mean, some people would say the same thing about me, that I have a way of infuriating folks. Whether it's true or not I'll plead guilty to it anyway. But that -- were you referring to by any chance to Mr. Beese?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But were you aware, and again I don't want to press you too much, but were you aware that -- that there had been meetings in early April, prior to your arrival, with Dr. Jadranko Prlic, between him and the ECMM, to resolve certain issues? And this was part of the process. In other words, you walked into this process. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Finally, if we can go to -- okay. I'm told -- okay. We're going to go to the next --

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me phrase it like this: I do not remember that I was aware of it. It was 14 years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. Very well. I'll skip one document. It's already in. We won't comment on it. I'm trying to be as judicious with my time as possible. Okay. The next topic deals with Mostar in general and the various issues. First of all, we touched upon a little bit the Vance-Owen Peace Plan, and if we could look at 1D 00892, and this is -- you will see that this is from a particular text. The first -- the second page shows that this is the Vance-Owen Plan, and it's on page 249?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hang on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But if we were to go all the way to the second to last page, and that would be on -- on 273, because if we were to flip through this you'll see that the Vance-Owen Peace Plan had various appendices to it and annexes, but at the -- on page 273 of this particular document, document 1D 00892, the Vance-Owen Peace Plan, we see where it says: "Province 8." I draw to everyone's attention and to your's, sir, where it says: "Province capital, Mostar," and then it says, "Governor nominated by party A. Vice governor nominated by party B." And then further down we see that there is something there for party C. And if we were to flip to page 2711, we see that party A refers to the Croats, party B to the Muslims and party C to the Serbs. Were you aware, sir -- this is my question, were you aware that at this part of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan, the way it had been envisaged, that Mostar would be the capital, the province capital, if you were, of province number 8? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand this was the Vance idea of a cantonal solution of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. But were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware of the cantonal plan, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But my question was rather more specific: Not so much whether you were aware that it was a cantonal plan but whether you were aware that Mostar would be the capital?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And I'm not suggesting that you should have been aware but I'm just going through that. If we go to P 02913. This is a letter. P 02913. P stands for "Prosecution."

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know. Mm-hmm. Is this in your document as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, it's in my documents. It will be in the Prosecution. We have it all there. It's sort of user-friendly, but I have an extra copy. Mr. Usher, can we get your assistance?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I've got them here. Number again, please.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. We're both electronic and manual here. Now if we look at it this is a letter dated 22 June 1993, and just -- if we just focus on the very first paragraph it shows that this is a letter to Lord Owen, and if we flip to the end we see that it's signed by Mate Boban, but we see as early as 22 June 1993, that Mate Boban is noting that the -- that it is impossible for the Muslims to be given Mostar, but they're talking -- the talk of this paper is about the union of republics. In other words, the discussions have already begun that within the greater Bosnia and Herzegovina there would be a union of republics. Were you aware of that, sir? As early as June 22nd.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably not in June 1993. I would guess I would not be in the picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well. If we go to 1D 01539. We're going back to Lord Owen. I won't be asking you to comment on personalities, but --

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number again, please.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And again, we're on page 226. If you go to the last paragraph, we note that he's talking about in Geneva on 20th of August, he says, "I brief EC missions and circulated the documents for a Bosnia settlement to which the leaders of the three parties had agreed in principle."

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't found that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. This is --

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes. The last --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I underscored that they agreed in principle. I think that's important so I don't want to mislead anybody that there was anything more than an agreement in principle. And it talks about the parties or the leaders having to consult with their parliaments. But if he would go to the next page, that is 227, which is on -- on the right side of -- of this page that you're looking at, sort of in the middle of that -- the first paragraph it says: "Mostar was to be placed under an EC administrator for up to two years along with -- along the same lines as UN administration of Sarajevo. Tudjman had been implacably opposed to UN control of Mostar, so I had suggested that the EC should take it on and Tudjman had accepted this across the negotiating table. Fortunately, the EC later backed me," and then it goes on. This is what I guess I'm trying to highlight. "It was agreed that part of the city would operate as the capital of the Croat majority republic." I underscore the word, it was agreed. Were you aware of that, sir? And this was as early as 20th of August, 1993. If you're not, that's fine and I understand you were not engaged in those negotiations.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were so many negotiations going on and the American negotiators were coming on stage and you had all sorts of information about solutions and I cannot state what I knew or did not know in the late summer 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. A bit like that old saying, too many cooks in the kitchen?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a way, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, I'm also a bit worried about the hearsay character of this. If there was an agreement, would there not be any document that would document this? This is just one person telling so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We're getting there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Good.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Remember, Your Honours, that this is a very long trial, but we're going to get there, and hopefully I will not disappoint. I try not to at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we go to the next document 1D 01557. And I just want -- this again is in his book. If we're fortunate we might cajole Lord Owen to grace us with his testimony here. But if we look at this, 1D 01557, you will see that on page 234 and page 235, it's on the same page --

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's 1557.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: 1557. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to follow it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You see that we have two maps.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I look at on the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir -- okay. You'll look at it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well. If you look at it -- the reason I'm pointing this out is we have two different maps, and we see that this is under the map 9, union of three republics, August 1993. If we look on the map and we see Mostar, we can see where it's located. And the same thing if we look at map 10. And it would appear at least -- it would give us an indication that Mostar at least by virtue of these maps was envisaged to be within the Croat-controlled area, if we want to put it that way, or within the Croat republic.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's a strange ring around Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: There is a strange ring and that may be because of the two years that the -- the EU, or the EC at the time --

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- administration. But were you aware of these maps?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So I'm not telling you anything that's new, and certainly I'm not stretching the facts as they were at the time you knew them?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt but just so the record is clear on this point, on map number 9, on the left side of the page, the legend or key to the map specifically does in fact indicate both Sarajevo and Mostar as being under EU administration under these plans. If you look at the key, the fourth box down from the top. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I think that Sarajevo would have been under the UN, but in any event I think the point is made and we thank --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have a map in my book which is the map made by the Contact Group.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which is another group and depicts Sarajevo in a completely different situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: So there are a number of maps. You will always find one that suits your purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Very well. Thank you for bringing that to our attention. So this sounds like reasonable doubt as far as when it comes to maps and lines.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I point that to the Court's attention. 1D 00526. This document, sir, 1D 00526. If you don't have it, we'll provide it for you. This is the Stoltenberg-Owen plan, and -- have you found it sir?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I may have it. Hang on. Hang on for a moment. 526.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Usually they're numbered in sort of a sequential order. All right. Now, if we look at the second page, which would -- which on the top left hand it says 276, we see again where Mostar is. This is a map of Bosnia-Herzegovina, union of republics of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and this is in the Stoltenberg-Owen plan. Then if we could -- if we could go to 3 -- 303. Incidentally, on that one page, that one map I showed you was very similar to what we saw earlier as to where Mostar is; correct? We see the ring around it. And again it would appear to be within the Croat-controlled republic.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Page 303?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, if we go to 303. Now, this is my next question. Number 65, appendix II, it talks about the agreed arrangements concerning the constitutional agreement of the union of republics of Bosnia-Herzegovina. First question is, were you aware of the Stoltenberg-Owen plan?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in principle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If not in detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Were you aware of this particular agreement or this agreed arrangement that appears to be part and parcel of the Stoltenberg-Owen plan, that is appendix II?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which agreement are you referring to? There was no agreement about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, this is the -- this is a plan that is being put forward, and it talks about agreed arrangements --

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- concerning the constitutional agreement.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I mention that because this was an ongoing process. And if we go to page 306, 306. We're taking the step-by-step process. That's why it's taking us a little bit longer, but hopefully part of the agreed arrangement -- if we look under B, Mostar City Opstina, and we see under 1 that there is an interim period. Number 2, that the European Community participation in the governance of the Mostar city opstina is planned for two years. We already talked about that. And then if we go to 3, and I want to highlight this for the Trial Chamber and maybe perhaps you can elucidate a little bit on it, "Mostar City Opstina which shall have within it the buildings of the capital of the Croat majority republic shall have the government function -- the governmental function and powers specified for constituent republics in the constitutional agreement." Were you aware that this was envisaged, that Mostar, Mostar city opstina, would be the capital or part of it would be the capital for the Croat majority republic?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As part of this plan, yes, but what is the date of this paper?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's a good -- 30th of September I'm told. But you were aware that this was an ongoing negotiating process?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And that the negotiators themselves, starting with the -- with Vance -- with Mr. Vance and Mr. Owen -- or Lord Owen, had envisaged that Mostar would be a capital city for the Croats in one way or another; correct?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The first paper you showed me was the canton.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: For number 8?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: For number 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But then --

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which is not the Croat republic. It was of a completely different solution for Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Exactly. Exactly. And I'm glad that you pointed that out. I'm happy. I'm delighted that you pointed that out, because we submit to the Trial Chamber at some point arguments will be made that when the community, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna moves to the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna is as a direct result of the ongoing peace process in anticipation that you would have a Bosnia-Herzegovina with three republics contained therein with Mostar being the capital of the Croatian republic. But thank you for drawing that to our attention. Now if we could go --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, would you be so kind to explain to us the expression Mostar opstina, Mostar city opstina because I don't think we have come across it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Delayed gratification, Your Honour. We're going to get there with my next section.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Okay, but I think it's better to explain a new term when it comes up and not refer to later when it is in another context.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It would have been step-by-step. It would have been first to explain the term and then use it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I apologise, Your Honour. I apologise. And you're right. As a technician, I should have -- I should have covered that. But let's go to page 308 of the document where we are talking about -- we see at the bottom there are attachments under B. "The outer boundary of the Mostar City Opstina." And then I'm going to hopefully describe it to you, Your Honour, in sort of pictorial terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It says here -- Mr. Usher, can we get your assistance here? "It has been suggested," it says over here in this document, "that the Mostar city opstina be defined as including the six," and here's where my pronunciation is rather poor, "mjesna zajednica" and then it lists "Aleksa Santic, Carina, Cernica, Brankovac, Donja Mahala, and Luka." And now if we look at the map, if we look at it, hopefully you will be able to see it, and if you have to move it -- you will have to move it, sir, a little bit further up and then over. There you go. There you go. Hold it. Now, it then goes on in the text: "This needs, however, to be determined by consultation in Mostar with all interested parties." And it goes on and so on. Were you aware that this was envisaged as the part of -- of what would be the Mostar city opstina?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. If I had been aware, I think it would have facilitated my endeavours to delineate the area for the EU administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Could we get an IC number for this document? And if we could go on --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, this document will become Exhibit IC 595.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if we could go very quickly to 1D 01551. Again we're going back to the "Balkan Odyssey" by David Owen. Now we're on page 252. And on the top of the page we see on 9 December he talks about having visited with Stoltenberg, Belgrade, and had a meeting with Milosevic, followed by a private meeting with -- with Karadzic and his team and Sarinic, President Tudjman, and so on. Further down it says: "At that meeting, we had made real progress on the map with the Croats being ready to accept the Neretva River as far south as Tasovici as the dividing line between the Muslim and Croat-majority republics and with Mostar still to be administered by the EU. But Silajdzic sent a depressing message which arrived during the meeting saying that the Muslims wanted Neum and were longer interested in having an outlet to the sea at Prevlaka as put forward by the Croats. Also, Izetbegovic could no longer come to the proposed meeting ..." And it goes on and on. And I think basically we want to go further down where we see: "We later invited them all to go on from Geneva to Brussels so that the parties could again meet with the foreign ministers in the hope that this would engender a better mood. We had by this time given up on being able to negotiate over Sarajevo and were resigned to having -- to having to have UN administration and in postponing this most difficult of all issues." Now, I skipped one portion which said earlier, the text says: "We therefore cancelled that meeting," meaning the meeting with Izetbegovic, "in favour of the one at Geneva on the morning of 21 December; but it was a bad sign and we look it to mean that the Bosnian Muslims wanted to go on fighting the Bosnian Croats and as yet felt under pressure to negotiate -- felt under no pressure to negotiate." Let me ask you because you've been asked by the Prosecution to talk about your impressions and the moods at the time. Would it be correct to say that at that time in history in theatre, because of what was happening on the ground with the Muslims gaining ground that they seemed to be obstructing or dragging their feet in trying to find any reasonable solution in ending the war between themselves and the Croats?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You make a lot of propositions, and you want me to answer yes or no. I can't do that on that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware of that when the luck of war shifted it immediately influenced the will of the parties to negotiate, because if you are on the winning side you want to delay decisions as long as possible to have a better hand. So I think it is correct what David Owen writes here. There was far less inclination for Muslims in December to come to the negotiating table than it was in April, and that explains also the situation in Mostar in April 1993, that they were far more willing to seek a solution at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. And would it be fair to say that one of the reasons was because, as we say in America, possession is nine tenths of the law. In other words --

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is extremely hard to negotiate another solution when the armies are standing on the ground when you make a cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So the more land you can capture, the more land you control, the better bargaining position you're in?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And just very briefly if we flip the page to 255, just flip it, you'll see that there is a map there. The EU Action Plan December 1993 - February 1994. And again if we take a look at where Mostar is placed on the EU -- or this is probably better -- I don't know if the EU existed at the time, but the EU action plan. Were you aware of this map, the EU action plan map?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we can move on to -- just one second. If we could go to P 0 -- yes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm still puzzled on this map, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Which map is that, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: The one you have just referred to on page 255.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. The action plan map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes. I'm probably mistaken, but what I see is a legend, and it -- this legend first says it's the action plan comprising that on the territory -- Muslim majority, and we have one area, which is area 2, and that has -- here it is indicated 65.49 per cent Muslim majority, and Mostar would be placed in that area. That seems to be not quite in line with what we have seen on other maps. So probably you could -- you could clarify or let the witness clarify this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I see the map -- if I may?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It only depicts the area that should be under Muslim governance, and it does not take up the -- how to divide between Serb and Croats. But I'm also very skeptic about the origin of this map and what makes an EU action plan and what importance it has. Is it a Dutch map in EU, or what is it? It seems to me to be out of context as I know the negotiations at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Does that answer Your Honour's question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes. I think it's probably a Serb/non-Serb map rather than a map which is similar to the ones we have seen before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, at the time -- at the time they were searching for a solution in order to -- based on percentages, and if you look on page 254, we're looking at -- you see the figure of 33.3 for the Muslim republic, and so -- because as the case progresses we'll see that during the negotiations the actual percentage of land became very important to all sides, but that was what was envisaged.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- I can tell the Court that I was heavily involved in drawing maps for David Owen and about percentages and the census from March 1991, I think, of the old opstinas. So there was a lot of percentage talk among the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. And if we fast forward to, I believe, Dayton there they had some sort of fancy apparatus where they were able to redraw the lines and calculate with exactitude so that all parties were -- were happy at the end of the day. You might recall that. To 49, 51; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we go to the -- the next document very quickly, P 07866. And the significance, basically, just very quickly, I just want to point out if we go to what -- to page 4, this is a report of the co-chairman of the steering committee on the activities of the International Conference on the Former Yugoslavia. And as we can see from the very first page it's 14 February 1994. But if we go to page 4, "Talks in Geneva 10 to 12 February." And then we just -- if we just flip the next page, under paragraphs 15, 16, and 17 -- perhaps we could skip 15 and 16 and just go straight to 17. "With regard to the definition of the Mostar city area to be placed under the administration of the European Union, the Bosnian Presidency and the Bosnian Croats agreed to a working group which had been established in Brussels on 23 December to look into this issue should meet on 16 February in Medjugorje at the headquarters of the Spanish Battalion." Now, you were part -- were you part of that process, the working group process?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If this is what the -- my meetings in Medjugorje were a part of, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So this was all part of the -- the ongoing negotiating process to find a solution between the Croats and the Muslims --

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- particularly with respect to the issue of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, very quickly since the Court has been kind enough to extend me some time I can get to my last chapter rather quickly. You were shown -- at the beginning of today, the Prosecution showed you document 752, which was Resolution 787. If you don't have it, we have it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, quickly. I don't mean to order you, but we're running out of the time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we look at the very last paragraph, it says here: "Noting --" on the first -- the very first page.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: "Noting the progress made so far within the framework of the international conference, including the joint declaration signed at Geneva on 30 September 1992," and it goes on, but if I just focus you to number 3: "The joint communique issued on 1 November 1992 at Zagreb by the presidents of the Republic of Croatia and the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina." And then it talks about, number 4, the establishment of a Mixed Military Working Group in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the production of a draft outline constitution for the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Now, were you aware, sir, of this joint communique that they're speaking about in this document of 1 November 1992?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. If we could go to the next document, 1D 01543. 1543. This is -- it's titled -- it's titled, if you look at the second page of this document it says: "Annex, Joint Communique issued on 1 November 1992" and talks between the president of the Republic of Croatia and the president of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And of course on the first page we see the date is 2nd of November, 1992 and makes reference to this joint communique. Would it be fair to say that this is the same communique that is being referenced in Resolution 787, which was shown to you by the Prosecution this morning?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It seems obvious.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we look at the very first page, which is actually page 2, but the annex, it says in the second paragraph that they reviewed, they being Tudjman and Izetbegovic: "They reviewed the implementation of the friendship and cooperation agreement between the two countries and discussed a number of topical issues ..." And -- so I just want to make sure I highlight that point, Friendship and Cooperation Agreement. Were you aware that there had been an agreement between the two countries, the two republics at that time? The Friendship and Cooperation Agreement, were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. I --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Don't --

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recollect exactly this joint communique, but because I knew about the talks in a way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This came just as I came to the theatre.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now if we can go to the fourth paragraph, I want to point out one thing --

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just point out that there was no lack of good documents and peaceful talk during this period from any of the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I agree. Now, if we go to the fourth paragraph, at the very last line it talks about that -- I'll read the last two sentences: "Joint unbiased commissions will be set up to determine individual responsibility." Then it goes on it state: "Similar occurrences will be avoided in the future through proper actions including urgent formation of a Joint Command of armed forces of BH army and HVO." So here we can see that as early as 2 November 1992 they're talking about a -- a joint command of the two forces.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: And nothing of it took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand that but --

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which is the essence, I think, with what we are to deal with here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Very well. We'll move on to the next document then, because I think it's important to look at what this agreement's all about, the agreement on Friendship and Cooperation. So if you could please turn to P 00339. P 00339. It's the Prosecution document. It's dated July 21, 1992. And regrettably we don't have too much time to -- to -- if we could go through to paragraph number 6. [Microphone not activated] Number 6 it says: "The armed component of the Croatian Defence Council (Hrvatsko Vijece Obrane) is an integral part of the united armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The Croatian Defence Council will have its representatives in the Joint Command of the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina." Question: Were you aware, sir, were you aware that the HVO was an integral part?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, I think we need to make this completely clear what was going on in the beginning of 1992 when the Croatian and the Muslim side joined forces and fought the Serbs, for example, in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Evicted the Serbs, ruined a number of Serb villages together, and they had every idea of going together at that time. Once that problem was solved, we come into the realities where I come into the picture, which happens a year later. So referring to the good intentions spelled out in early 1992, I think, has very little bearing on what happened in April 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Can you produce me a document, sir, that at any point in time this agreement on Friendship and Cooperation was renounced?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you produce me any documents about any agreements being denounced on the Balkans?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir, I'm asking the questions here.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So the -- so the answer is no. During that period of time while you were there and before you arrived, is it not a fact that the Republic of Croatia was assisting in the arming of the -- of the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Is that not one form of -- of the friendship agreement? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It might well be, but it can also be that your enemy is my friend.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well. But -- you know, usually you don't arm your enemy at the same time while your enemy is attacking you; right? I mean, it's an unusual circumstance?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even that happened at time on the Balkans.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now, if we get to paragraph number 8, and I think that we're just going to cover -- I'll just read it: "In consideration of the continuing aggression of Serbian Montenegrin military forces against the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but also largely against the Republic of Croatia from the contiguous areas of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the president of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the president of the Republic of Croatia call upon the international community and in particular the United Nations, the European Community, and the United States of America, to take real and efficient steps to vigorously stop the aggression against their States, to prevent further loss of human life, persecution and expulsion of their citizens and the destruction of property." Question: At that point in time in history, was the parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina used as a staging ground for a foreign army to be attacking the Republic of Croatia? Yes, no, I don't know?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: What date are we talking about here?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, this was signed 20 -- 21st July 1992.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer is probably yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: But, Mr. Karnavas, isn't this outside the time when the witness was engaged in Bosnia-Herzegovina? I think you strongly opposed --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: -- when later, and I think we have to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: -- have cautious approach to the answer then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand that, but then the Trial Chamber allowed the gentleman to answer the questions of the Prosecution. Now, I can ask a couple of preparatory questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir, before going into theatre, did -- to work for the UN, that is, especially given your high-ranking position within the UN, and in keeping with the answer that you gave us just earlier where you were able to recall prior to your arrival what the Muslims and Croats were doing, is it fair to say that you knew exactly what had been going on in and about the various republics of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No? Okay. So earlier when you were saying -- what about Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you talking about what I knew before I came to theatre?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I did not fully knew what was going on in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you know what was happening in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I didn't. It doesn't -- I had friends serving in Mostar. One of my best friends was serving in Mostar during this period when the fighting was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: While you were in theatre, did you learn what had happened or were you merely speculating earlier when you were saying that the Croats and the Muslims gathered -- got together to repel the Serbs at a point in time when you were not there? Were you?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Were you taking a wild guess?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I have valid information about what took place in Mostar during the fighting because a colleague from my own regiment was the UN observer in Mostar and played a substantial role in bringing out women and children during that fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: So I have some ideas what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And you must have known what the JNA was doing?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And you must have known what the JNA was doing to the republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And where it was operating from.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, I don't think I knew that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In July --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Later on did you find out?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later on --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please kindly avoid overlapping.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, yes. When I came on stage there was very little fighting going on in Croatia between the two parties. It had settled down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Was their land occupied?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Who was occupying it?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The so-called self-proclaimed state of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And who was supporting them?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did that still pose a threat to the Zagreb government?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we could go on with this document, because the Friendship Agreement goes on to state: "With this objective in mind, both states will sustain their past successful cooperation and continuous cooperation -- coordination of the defensive activities in the contiguous zones of the two states." Was that ever brought to your attention?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This specific paragraph, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. That they were coordinating the defensive activities.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So while you were there -- granted you showed up -- I believe it was November 1992, all the way until November 1993 when you were with UNMO, this was not brought to your attention? I mean -- I'm not suggesting that it should have been, but I'm just wondering whether you were aware of it.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This specific document I don't think I read at the time. I don't recollect having read it, anyway. I think my image starting around Christmas 1993 was not one of intimate cooperation between the Croats and the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. And if we just go on to the last paragraph. "Aware of the fact that both states are threatened, unless aggression against them is urgently stopped by further destruction and annihilation of their --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Excuse me. Mr. Karnavas, I'm sorry to interrupt you. The General said just a minute ago that I think my image starting around Christmas 1993 was not one of intimate cooperation between the Croats and the Muslims. And I wonder, General, if you meant 1993 or 1992?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: 1992. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, when you say Croats, you're talking about Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Was there still contact between Mr. Izetbegovic and Mr. Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Was Croatia still continuing at that point in time to receive refugees --

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- from Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Many of those refugees were Muslim?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we go on, it says here: "Aware of the fact that both states are threatened, unless aggression against them is urgently stopped, by further destruction and annihilation of their state entity and integrity, the two states will, should the efforts of the international community remain ineffective, take all necessary steps in order to establish broader cooperation in the military sphere and coordinate military operations in order to definitely repel the danger threatening them." Now, were you aware of that, that this is what was envisaged by these two gentlemen, at least back in July 21, 1992?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no difficulty imagining that because the Serb offensive, I would say, was ongoing, and all -- as you indicated, even during Christmastime in 1992 there were a lot of refugees coming out, especially from the Banja Luka area into Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: So we were under a period of Serb aggression at that time when they were gaining hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. Now, if we could just go back to document 752. This was Resolution 787 that we -- that we looked at when we began.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, just one question I'd like to put to you. This document 00339, I believe that this document has already been tendered. This friendship and cooperation agreement between the two republics, we can see that this document was signed in the B/C/S version is -- as far as you know, was this document published in the Official Gazette of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and in the Official Gazette of Croatia, and do you know whether this document was forwarded to the Secretary-General of the United Nations since this document refers to all the resolution that were taken since the 15th of July, 1992, and among others, Resolution 752?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the answer to your first -- to the first part of your question was I believe no, it wasn't published in the Official Gazette. And with respect to the latter part of your question, I believe I might be able to answer that in due course. I know it may not be satisfactory, but that's the best I can do under the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I have acknowledged what you have said. There is -- this is not an urgent matter, but another question. Under the laws of Bosnia-Herzegovina, what governed international treaties? We can consider that this agreement would be part or come under the heading of international treaties. How does this work? Is there a ratification procedure? President Tudjman and President Izetbegovic, did they not have to submit this document in parliament or discuss it in parliament? You don't answer any of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I'm not it at this point in time, but Mr. Izetbegovic was there on behalf of the Presidency and we have touched on it a little bit. While he is being referred to as the president of Bosnia-Herzegovina, he was never that. He was president of the Presidency, and he was -- and at the time the Presidency was responsible due to the conditions of making all major decisions at the state level. And of course I can't speak for Mr. Tudjman, but again I take your question on board and in due course we will answer that because we do think that is an important issue to clarify for the Trial Chamber. I just have one final question or two with -- related -- related back to Resolution 787.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir, do you have that document with you?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well. If we could go to paragraph number 5. That would be on page 3. And I just want to point this out where it says -- we see here that it "demands that all forms of interference from outside the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, including infiltration," you touched on this a little bit, "into the country of irregular units and personnel, cease immediately and reaffirms its determination to take measures against all parties and others concerned which fail to fulfil the requirements of Resolution 752 and its other relevant resolutions, including the requirement that all forces, in particular elements of the Croatian army, be withdrawn, or be subject to the authority of the government of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, or be disbanded or disarmed." Now, if we go back to what we were talking about earlier with -- in the friendship agreement where it noted that the Croatian -- that the HVO was an integral part of the united armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, would it not follow, then, that elements of the Croatian army could be subordinated to the HVO and would fulfil the requirement of paragraph 5 of Resolution 787, because after all the HVO at that point in time, given the friendship agreement, was considered part and partial of the legitimate armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Are you suggesting --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, General, before you answer. Your Honour, a couple of things. One I'm not sure that this witness can answer in any event; but secondly, I really wonder if the time comes when -- are now conceding that there were Croatian army elements in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1992, which is the only possible foundation for Mr. Karnavas's question, or is this mere speculation? If it's the second then there is no value in it, but I think the time has to come when either the Croatian army is in Bosnia and Herzegovina subject to certain agreements or it's not in Bosnia and Herzegovina but we can't have it both ways at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may respond very briefly. We've heard testimony that you had Croats from Bosnia and Herzegovina who were living in Croatia, who might have been in the Croatian army, who came back to their homeland, to their villages, to their areas to serve in the HVO. And it would appear that given the friendship agreement, that it would have been perfectly legitimate for those individuals to come and serve, and it would have been perfectly proper and within paragraph 5 of Resolution 787. We're talking about soldiers. So when I say elements, well, a soldier might be an element. Now, Judge Trechsel, I mean, I'm going at the lowest form of an element.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, can I respond, please? The clear -- what -- the clear thrust of the examination for the last few minutes is indicating that it was Tudjman on behalf of the Croatian government that apparently entered into a partnership or a friendship agreement. These weren't individual -- individual soldiers that had grown up in Siroki Brijeg and decided to go back. This was the president of the Republic of Croatia, and the elements -- Resolution 752 and the other documents we've looked at in addition to talking in some instances about individuals talk about the Croatian army, the regular Croatian army. And I come back to my original -- to my previous point. The time has come either the Croatian army was in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and if Mr. Karnavas wants to say it was pursuant to a friendship agreement so be it, but they were there, or they were not there but we can't have it both ways. The Croatian army was not -- there in Bosnia and not in Bosnia at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it -- first of all, I bear --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, would you ask your questions, because in paragraph 5 it speaks of irregular units and also there is the word "personnel." So I might think that beyond regular units, legal units, there might also have been some personal behaviours of individuals. Very well. So please ask directly the question to the general. Your question is very complicated. I think he's capable of answering it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Let me go step-by-step. You had heard my original question and I think that you wanted to answer or you were about to answer, but do you feel confident that --

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Will you've rephrased that question, because you have had long argument and I'm a senile man so I almost forgot it now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: From your answers one would not call you senile, but very well. At least -- we looked at the friendship agreement, and in the friendship agreement it's quite clear that the HVO, not the HV but HVO, was an integral part of the -- of the forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina. An integral part of the united armed forces. So that would mean, at least from the friendship agreement, that Izetbegovic recognises the HVO to be part and partial of the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Now we go to paragraph 5 of Resolution 787, and the portion that I'm most interested in where it talks about: "Including the requirement of all forces, in particular elements of the Croatian army, be withdrawn or be subject to the authority of the government of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, or be disbanded or disarmed." Now, Judge Trechsel was taken aback when I said even soldiers could be considered an element, but under this -- this paragraph, would it not stand to follow that you could have a unit of the Croatian army that placed itself under the HVO and would be in compliance of paragraph 5 of this particular resolution, keeping in mind the friendship agreement wherein Izetbegovic recognises the HVO as part and parcel of the legitimate armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, my objection is the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My objection is the same.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please don't overlap.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, just to be consistent with the point that I've been trying to make for the last 15 minutes or so. Again, it's either -- is there any evidence that actually ever happened, and in which case, then the Croatian army was in Bosnia and Herzegovina; or is this mere speculation of something that never happened? And if it is the latter, there is no value in putting the question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, my question doesn't deal with facts; it deals with whether the gentleman, in light of his education, background, experience, is able to draw a conclusion. Now, if he's not able and if that is what the Prosecution's objection is, that is, that he is not competent to answer the question because he lacks either personal knowledge or lacks the ability to -- lacks the ability to put two and two together as I'm doing, then fine. I understand that the gentleman is not a lawyer, but I'm not asking him to venture so far out into legal land where he has to divine what might be in this particular resolution, because after all it was the Prosecutor that was showing him resolution after resolution and the gentleman had no problem in answering the question. So if he's not able to answer the question, then I withdraw the question; I'll sit down.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I have no problem with showing the witness resolutions, as indeed the Prosecution did. I have no objection to the witness answering reasonable questions at all. My objection is whether -- let me rephrase it. Not my objection, but then based on what Mr. Karnavas has said, the question to the witness is: Would it have been possible, would it have been possible, for an HV unit to subordinate itself to the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Whether it ever happened or not, the question, then, is it possible it could have happened that an HV unit could have subordinated itself to the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina. If that's the question, then I think certainly the witness can answer it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, that's not the question, and Mr. Scott can ask that question on redirect. In fact, if he does ask it on redirect, I promise not to object. But my question is rather more precise, and my question is, in light of the friendship agreement, in light of what is happening in the situation, keeping in mind that you have Croats who are living in -- across from Bosnia and Herzegovina, who are living in Croatia, who might have been serving in the Croatian army who now may wish to go back and fight in their homelands, assuming that you had a unit of the Croatian army - I'm not saying that was the case; I'm just saying assuming - if that unit were to subordinate itself, as is demanded under paragraph 5 to the HVO, keeping in mind that the HVO is recognised by Mr. Izetbegovic as being an integral part, one of the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina, would that not be in compliance of this particular paragraph?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Not only is your question terribly complicated, but also it hangs sort of in the air. You start from an agreement purportedly between two states, or at least two "head of states."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Then you talk about a unit submitting itself to another army. That would not be an act of one of the states or the president of the states. It's different if the president decides, pursuant to an agreement, to dispatch part of his army to serve abroad. But a -- and then your patriotic spontaneous fighters, how can they be withdrawn? The Security Council cannot have had those in mind at all. So it would be helpful if you could sort of put short questions step by step instead of speaking for half a page and then nobody knows what any answer would actually mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm trying to help. I hope you noticed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I noticed that, Your Honour, but again, we're not talking about one army subordinating itself under another army. It says here "particular elements." What is a particular element of the Croatian army? In my definition, a particular element could be a single soldier who wants to go back to his village which is under threat. That could be an element. And it seems to me that the UN over here - and maybe this is something for closing argument - but it seems to me what the UN is saying here, as long as that element places itself, subordinates itself within the lawful army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, everything is copacetic. And if the HVO is part and parcel of the armed forces, the legitimate armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina, it would stand to reason that soldiers who might have left, you know, Croatia and joined the HVO would have been perfectly fine. There's no nefariousness to that. Now, that's the nature of my question. If it's too complicated, then the gentleman can certainly tell me it's too complicated and he can't answer it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First, a comment. It does not say particular elements of a Croatian army. It says "in particular, elements of a Croatian army," which is quite another thing, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, in particular elements. But what is an element? It doesn't specify what elements are. Would you agree with me on that, sir?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It doesn't speculate if it is a brigade or a battalion or a platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Or a couple of soldiers?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or a couple of soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: But they are elements of a Croatian army. They are wearing the uniforms of a Croatian army. They are subordinates of a Croatian army. And your interpretation must imply, as far as I understand, that this agreement of Mr. Tudjman and Izetbegovic should overrule a UN resolution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I'm not asserting anything of the kind. I'm just merely asking you one --

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the only way to make it legal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I believe I've exhausted this area, Mr. President. I want to thank the Judges for allowing me the extra time to go into this, and hopefully we'll clarify it with others. Sir, I want to thank you very much for coming here to give your evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I trust that I wasn't too combative with you. You're a general. I'm just a mere Defence lawyer. I'm sure you can handle yourself. Thank you again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'd like to inform you that I have one hour accorded me by the Trial Chamber, and I have been given 15 minutes from the Pusic Defence and 15 minutes from the Coric Defence. So according to my calculations, that would mean that I have until the end of the working day today. But I'll do my best to go through the basic topics and complete them as quickly as possible. However, if I don't manage to get through everything that I've planned, then I'll go on tomorrow morning and would like to ask the Trial Chamber to give me an extra 20 minutes to Mr. Murphy in order to deal with some questions which step outside the framework of my cross-examination. So I just wanted to inform you about that in advance, and the Trial Chamber can think about it and give a ruling tomorrow. I think you've all received copies of my documents. The witness has, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So let me say: Good afternoon to you, sir. I'm going to try and speak slower to help our interpreters, and we have provided them with copies of our documents, but let me introduce you. My name is Senka Nozica, and Mr. Peter Murphy and I are the Defence counsel for Mr. Bruno Stojic. And for that reason I'm going to take you back to some other topics, the topics of the meeting held on the 18th of April about which you have spoken at length. Now, during the examination-in-chief, you said that the meeting of the 18th of April, 1993, began before your arrival and Mr. Ganic's arrival in Mostar; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: After that, you went on to say that you left the meeting with Mr. Petkovic so that you could talk to him about his insistence upon having Mr. Halilovic attend the discussions and the agreement to be reached; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Upon your return to the conference hall, you met Mr. Stojic there, who said that the Muslims had undertaken some attacks in Central Bosnia and addressed Mr. Ganic and said that he wouldn't leave Mostar alive; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Sir, before that had you ever met Mr. Stojic?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: No. Right. Do you know, sir, how this debate started?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which debate?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm referring to what Mr. Stojic started off by saying and the response to him by someone else with respect to the arguments he put forward.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear any response to his arguments for the moment when he was in the room.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Do you know whether Mr. Stojic said specifically what information he had received about the events in the territory where the offensive by the BH army began?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he was specific, but I do not remember which areas he mentioned. But he was specific about points.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Do you perhaps happen to know what Mr. Ganic said to him in response to his allegations?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember that Ganic said anything. He might have done it, but I have no recollection of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Is it possible that Mr. Ganic might have said something before your arrival in the conference hall? Because as far as I understood you, you entered the hall while the discussion was already under way.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And I'd like to ask you, to the best of your recollections, whether that meeting was in fact interrupted, because you said that it was interrupted and cut short by Mr. Stojic, or was it put off and delayed for some reason?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my recollection is that after Mr. Stojic went out, we, so to say, went out of this meeting and it was finished. I don't remember the exact words that Ambassador Thebault used to finish the meeting, but it was finished in a way. And it was Prlic who stood up first and excused -- or apologised for the words that had been uttered. And then I think we just closed the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you remember that at the meeting some agreement was reached? I'm asking you all this because you yourself said that you didn't attend part of the meeting. Now, do you know whether any agreements were reached?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You also said during the examination-in-chief that the following day, that is to say, on the 19th of April, 1993, you were called by Mr. Stojic and apologised.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure about the dates. I think I went to see General Petkovic first on that day, and -- so I have to see the statements to be exactly clear whether I saw Stojic on the 19th or the 20th. But I went to see him anyway one of these days, when I was called in a meeting that he wanted to see me.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes. That's what you've said in your statement. Yesterday, it would appear that it was on the following day, but that's not essential. It was either on the 19th or the 20th anyway. That's quite certain, during those two days while you were in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You said that on that occasion Mr. Stojic said that you shouldn't believe and trust the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You also said that Mr. Stojic on that same occasion during that conversation mentioned certain places in the north, specific ones, and I'm talking about the second conversation which was -- should be in the focus of attention and interest before Mostar, and that that was the first time that you heard that insistence was made on some other localities outside Mostar. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think that probably General Petkovic touched on these things when we talked in this morning meeting. So I think this was a repetition but perhaps more forcefully put forward.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes. And I found that in the report for that day, that is to say the 18th, that you said that Mr. Petkovic mentioned the Jablanica region and Konjic. Yes, and Konjic too. And that is why I am insisting upon this. But if you say that Mr. Stojic insisted upon it again, that means that those were places and localities which for the Croatian side became highly significant. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But at the time I'm -- I don't, I think, fully understood that. I thought it was a trick to get attention away from Mostar more or less.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes, but -- yes, precisely, but you understood this as drawing your attention away from Mostar, but you also said that at the 19th of April, 1993, meeting an agreement was reached whereby Mostar, Jablanica, Konjic, and Sovici should be toured. I think this you said that during the examination-in-chief yesterday. Now, for that reason, would it emerge that that information provided sufficient grounds for placing Jablanica and Konjic as the focal point?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did. Both parties agreed on these areas later on with Pasalic and Lasic. There was complete agreeance between the parties on what points were of essential interest, actually. And the Konjic and Jablanica were among them.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So can we now say that this endeavour, these efforts on the part of Mr. Stojic and Mr. Petkovic, to focus on these other places as well was not drawing your attention away from Mostar but, rather, the demand that this be placed on a par with them, on the same level, because according to their information, an offensive by the Muslim army had already started up there. So could we say that those places deserved equal attention within the frameworks of your mission, just like Mostar did?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but not more.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we'll come back to that to see whether they were more or less, whether those adjectives could be applied, but -- I'd like to know when we're going to take the break, because I have two more questions before the break to ask within this area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So nothing happened to Mr. Ganic despite the threats; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Nobody attacked him?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he was in a UN vehicle when we least Mostar, so it would have been astonishing if anybody had attacked him. I don't think he was in danger that day, actually. I never took it really seriously.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I see, yes. That's important for me. You said you never took it really seriously. Well, you told Mr. Lasic if he didn't carry out his promise about the cease-fire that probably this would follow him to hell. Now, you spent a lot of time in the south, I'm not going to say in the Balkans, but in the south, the area that I live in, the territory I live in, sophisticated threats of that nature are not used. What is used is quite blatant threats, but they have the same idea as what you said, that you would pursue him to the gates of hell or --

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't carry a sidearm on my side, and I made it through an interpreter. It was quite another situation, and I -- so if you threaten to kill a member of the Presidency and you wear a sidearm at the same time you do that, it is another threat situation, actually. So don't try to compare it. I didn't scare Lasic a bit, but Ganic was extremely scared, and he has explained to me later that I saved his life that day. End of quotation.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Sir, I'm sure you'll agree with me when I say that from what you yourself said, Mr. Stojic did not threaten Mr. Ganic that he would kill him, but the threat was uttered in a very general manner. Now, when you say that Mr. Ganic told you that you'd saved his life, where in fact did he go, and when did he leave the Mostar area, in fact?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me wait a minute, Your Honour. Let's have -- instead of having just a statement and then no question, let's have the witness respond to counsel's assertion. Counsel has just asserted there was no threat against Mr. Ganic by Mr. Stojic, but then she states that as an assertion and then goes to the next question. Let's have the witness give the answer whether there was a threat against Mr. Ganic or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the witness gave his answer. The witness did answer. I heard it, but I can't see that it's in the record. The witness did give an answer to my question when I asked him whether Mr. Stojic issued threats or whether he made an observation that he wouldn't leave Mostar alive, the witness said yes. But that wasn't recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me I'm sorry for interrupting. I don't see anything of an answer on -- on line -- page 88 anywhere around line 14, 15, or 16. I don't see any answer to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ask the question again.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to interpret this. I merely observed that Mr. Stojic did not threaten that he would kill Mr. Ganic, but he just made the assertion. Do you agree with me there?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said that Mr. Ganic would never leave Mostar alive. And if a man with a gun on his hip says those words, I would be rather offended if I had been Mr. Ganic. So he threatened him, all right. Then how serious it was one can discuss, and I at the moment didn't take it so serious, but obviously Mr. Ganic did. That was my point.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes, but -- yes. Yes. Yes. That's precisely what you said. "I didn't take it seriously, but Mr. Ganic obviously did." Now, after that I asked you when and where did Mr. Ganic go to linked to this threat?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, we took him in the Spanish armoured carrier and took him to the Spanish headquarter, and he later joined General Morillon and Ambassador Thebault and went to Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: When was that? Can you remember the date perhaps? When was that in relation to the meeting of the 18th of April?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose they might have left in the morning of the 20th if Morillon -- no. No. Well, let me put it this way: He stayed in Medjugorje until Morillon arrived, and he -- as far as I remember, he did not come with us into Mostar that night when we went down with Petkovic and Halilovic to meet the -- their subordinates. And if he was still in Medjugorje then, he should have left with Morillon next morning. So then we are probably on the 20th at least. But he has -- he has left my memory.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Sir, before the break let me just try and jog your memory. Can you -- do you remember that the next day, that is to say on the 19th of April, the day after the meeting, Ganic and Mr. Halilovic arrived at the meeting in the Ministry of Defence? Can you remember that, that that's what happened, that's how the events developed? And the day after, he went off with Mr. Morillon to Zenica.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
